title: Congenital torticollis (sternocleidomastoid mass, head tilt): intrauterine malposition
vignette: A 21-day-old boy is brought to the office by his mother because of a palpable bulge in the child's neck. He continues to feed well but appears comfortable only when held with his body sideways under the breast. He is at the 50th percentile for height, weight, and head circumference. The child favors looking toward the right and cries when his head is turned to the left. There is a firm mass on the left side of his neck that does not move when the child swallows. The remainder of the examination is unremarkable. Which of the following conditions was most likely present prenatally?

clues.text: favors looking toward the right and cries when his head is turned to the left
clues.note: A contracted left sternocleidomastoid tilts the head toward the left (affected) side and rotates the chin toward the RIGHT - the child resists turning back to the left.

clues.text: firm mass on the left side of his neck that does not move when the child swallows
clues.note: A firm SCM mass that does NOT move with swallowing (unlike a thyroglossal duct cyst) is the fibrotic sternocleidomastoid of congenital torticollis.

whatMatters: A firm sternocleidomastoid mass with head TILT toward the affected side and chin turned AWAY, appearing at 2-4 weeks, is CONGENITAL TORTICOLLIS - most commonly from INTRAUTERINE MALPOSITION (or birth trauma) causing sternocleidomastoid injury and fibrosis. Answer B.
strategy: Recognize congenital torticollis (SCM mass, characteristic head posture, weeks of age) and recall its usual cause: malposition of the head in utero (e.g., from macrosomia/oligohydramnios) or birth trauma -> SCM injury/fibrosis. Reject other prenatal exposures with different phenotypes: folate deficiency (neural tube defects), defective collagen synthesis (osteogenesis imperfecta - fractures), maternal alcohol (fetal alcohol syndrome - facial dysmorphism/growth deficits), and maternal URI/rubella (TORCH - hearing loss, cataracts, cardiac defects).

options.text: Upper respiratory infection in the mother

eliminations.label: Folate deficiency - neural tube defects
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: inadequate periconceptional folate. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it causes NEURAL TUBE DEFECTS (spina bifida, anencephaly), not a sternocleidomastoid mass/torticollis. ✅ Correct if: open neural tube defect.

eliminations.label: Defective collagen synthesis - osteogenesis imperfecta
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a type I collagen defect (osteogenesis imperfecta). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it causes brittle bones/fractures, blue sclerae, and hearing loss - not congenital torticollis. ✅ Correct if: multiple fractures with blue sclerae.

eliminations.label: Maternal alcohol - fetal alcohol syndrome
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: prenatal alcohol exposure. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: fetal alcohol syndrome causes growth restriction, smooth philtrum/thin vermilion, small palpebral fissures, and developmental deficits - not a neck mass/torticollis. ✅ Correct if: characteristic facies + growth/developmental deficits.

eliminations.label: Maternal URI/rubella - TORCH defects
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a maternal respiratory infection (e.g., rubella, a TORCH pathogen). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: rubella causes hearing loss, cataracts, and congenital heart defects (PDA), not congenital torticollis. ✅ Correct if: congenital rubella triad.

reasoning: A firm sternocleidomastoid mass (not moving with swallowing) with head tilt toward the affected side = congenital torticollis
It typically develops by 2-4 weeks of age
It most commonly results from intrauterine malposition (or birth trauma) injuring the sternocleidomastoid
mechanism: CONGENITAL (MUSCULAR) TORTICOLLIS typically becomes apparent by 2-4 WEEKS of age and is most commonly caused by BIRTH TRAUMA (e.g., breech/difficult delivery) or MALPOSITION of the head IN UTERO (e.g., from fetal macrosomia or oligohydramnios), both of which can INJURE the STERNOCLEIDOMASTOID (SCM) MUSCLE, leading to fibrosis and a firm palpable MASS in the inferior third of the SCM (this mass, unlike thyroid/thyroglossal lesions, does NOT move with swallowing). The contracture pulls the head into a characteristic posture: the head TILTS TOWARD the affected (contracted) SCM and the chin POINTS AWAY (toward the opposite side) - so a left SCM lesion produces a left head tilt with the chin/gaze toward the right, and the infant resists turning the head to the left. Associated musculoskeletal anomalies (hip dysplasia, metatarsus adductus, clubfoot) may coexist, and severe cases can cause plagiocephaly/facial asymmetry. Most resolve with conservative stretching. The distractors correspond to unrelated prenatal insults (neural tube defects, osteogenesis imperfecta, fetal alcohol syndrome, congenital rubella).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Peds > congenital torticollis: onset 2-4 weeks; birth trauma or in-utero malposition -> sternocleidomastoid injury/fibrosis; firm SCM mass (doesn't move with swallow); head tilts toward affected muscle, chin away; +/- hip dysplasia/clubfoot; treat with stretching.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: SCM mass + head tilt toward affected side (weeks old) = congenital torticollis from intrauterine malposition/birth trauma.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on congenital torticollis, sternocleidomastoid, head tilt vs chin rotation, plagiocephaly, or intrauterine malposition? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Folate = neural tube defects; collagen = osteogenesis imperfecta; alcohol = FAS; maternal URI/rubella = TORCH defects.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: congenital torticollis = SCM injury/fibrosis from in-utero malposition/birth trauma; head tilts toward, chin away; conservative stretching.

keywords.front: Firm SCM mass + head tilt in a newborn

keywords.back: Intrauterine malposition or birth trauma (SCM injury/fibrosis)
Tilts toward affected SCM; chin points away

memoryHook: A tight neck muscle from being cramped in the womb tugs the baby's head toward the sore side while the chin swings away - congenital torticollis.
